options: The maximum value a function can ever reach
The total area under a function's curve
The average value of a function over its entire domain
The instantaneous rate of change of a function at a specific point -- the slope of the graph at that exact point
questions.explain: A derivative is specifically the slope at one exact point, not an average slope over an interval or any other global property of the function.

questions.q: In the worked example, the numerical derivative (-0.43301270186146823) and the analytic derivative (-0.4330127018922193) agree to about 9 decimal places but not exactly. Why?
options: The two formulas are actually computing two completely unrelated quantities
The numerical approximation uses a small but finite step size h, introducing a tiny, expected approximation error, whereas the analytic formula is exact
This tiny disagreement means the analytic formula must be wrong
Node.js cannot perform calculus computations accurately under any circumstances
questions.explain: A numerical derivative approximates the true instantaneous rate of change using a small but nonzero step h, which introduces a small, well-understood approximation error -- the near-exact agreement is exactly what confirms the analytic formula is correct.

options: An equation relating a function to its own derivative (or higher derivatives)
An equation that can only be solved using a computer
Any equation that contains a fraction
An equation with no real-number solutions
questions.explain: A differential equation connects a function to how it changes (its derivative) -- this is the defining structural feature, distinct from an ordinary algebraic equation.

questions.q: What is the key structural pattern this lesson identifies behind both exponential decay (dN/dt = -kN) and the Schrodinger equation?
options: Both equations have no real-world physical meaning
The rate of change of the system depends on the system's own current state, not on some separate external time-varying input
Both equations can only be solved using the same specific numerical method
Both equations describe systems that never change over time
questions.explain: Both equations say 'how fast this changes right now depends on what it currently is' -- dN/dt depends on N itself, and the Schrodinger equation's d|psi>/dt depends on |psi> itself via the Hamiltonian.

questions.q: Why does recognizing the Schrodinger equation's structural pattern ('rate of change depends on current state via an operator') make it more approachable?
options: It's the exact same pattern already familiar from a simpler example (exponential decay), so the notation becomes a specific instance of something already understood rather than something entirely new
Recognizing the pattern has no real effect on how approachable the equation feels
It means the Schrodinger equation can be ignored entirely in later courses
It proves the Schrodinger equation is mathematically identical to exponential decay in every respect
questions.explain: Seeing the Schrodinger equation as the same 'rate of change depends on current state' pattern already seen in a simpler, familiar example makes the unfamiliar notation map onto something already understood, rather than being intimidating from scratch.
